papers.title: Monolith, porous bead, membrane or fibre? A comparative characterisation of four oligo-dT affinity chromatography matrices for mRNA capture
papers.abstract: Oligo-deoxythymidine (oligo dT) affinity chromatography is the most widely used capture step for in vitro transcribed mRNA and is now offered in four stationary-phase architectures, yet, to our knowledge, no published study has compared all four. We characterised a monolith, perfusive porous beads, a membrane adsorber and an electrospun cellulose fibre adsorber with a short (eGFP, 930 nt) and a long (SARS CoV 2 spike, S 2P, 4284 nt) mRNA. After screening the loading salt (NaCl or guanidine hydrochloride, Gu HCl), we mapped load flow rate, load concentration and Gu HCl concentration with response surface designs and compared the formats at near-optimal conditions. Gu HCl gave a higher peak recovery than NaCl in seven of the eight matrix construct combinations. At the near-optimal runs, the fibre adsorber recovered 17.9 mg eGFP and 13.3 mg S 2P per mL of bed, 2.3 to 2.6 fold the membrane and 3.5- to 4.8-fold the monolith and beads (p membrane > monolith > beads (0.314 to 0.035 mg/mL/min for eGFP). The membrane and fibre adsorber lost yield sharply above 0.4 to 0.6 M Gu HCl, whereas the monolith and beads declined gradually. In an amortised cost model at baseline cost inputs, the fibre adsorber was the least expensive format per milligram of purified mRNA at every number of device cycles (USD 114 to 140/mg for single use and 78 to 92/mg at 20 cycles), and the membrane the most expensive. A one at a time sensitivity analysis over wide ranges of the mRNA feed cost, the labour and facility rate, the device price and the number of cycles per device left the fibre adsorber the least expensive format in almost every combination examined, with the mRNA feed cost the dominant input. Only the monolith and beads are currently marketed as GMP grade, process scale materials, so the choice of format depends on whether capacity, productivity, cost or manufacturing readiness takes priority.

papers.title: Associations between structural and functional hemodynamics in the optic nerve head
papers.abstract: Purpose: Glaucoma is characterized by progressive degeneration of retinal ganglion cells axons thought to initiate within the optic nerve head (ONH). Although the precise mechanisms remain unclear, a leading hypothesis suggests that insufficient blood flow and oxygenation may be significant contributors to axonal damage. Measuring ONH oxygenation directly, however, is difficult. Hence, our first goal was to identify associations between structural and functional hemodynamics parameters (flow and oxygenation). We then evaluated whether local tissue oxygenation and hypoxia can be estimated from measurable parameters. Methods: Following previously reported methods, the ONH vasculature of four healthy monkey eyes was reconstructed. Numerical simulations were performed to determine blood flow and oxygen distribution. Structural parameters of each segment, including spatial location, orientation, length, and tortuosity, and functional hemodynamics parameters of each segment, including blood flow, pressure, blood oxygenation, and surrounding tissue oxygenation, were quantified. Results: Structural parameters exhibited no distinct spatial distribution, whereas hemodynamic and oxygenation parameters followed radial patterns. Although blood flow correlated with tissue oxygenation (p<0.001), regional mismatches indicated that flow alone was insufficient to predict accurately local oxygenation. We developed two multivariable mixed-effects models using measurable structural and flow parameters, a quadratic model that predicted continuous tissue oxygenation with high accuracy (R^2=0.75) and a logistic model that estimated local hypoxia risk. Conclusions: Our results provide a framework for estimating local tissue oxygenation and hypoxia risk that currently cannot be measured experimentally from vascular structural and flow parameters that can be measured.

papers.title: CT-Derived In Vitro Model Simulating Neonatal Cranial Growth
papers.abstract: Purpose: This study presents an in vitro platform for quantitatively simulating cranial growth in neonates from 3 to 6 months of age. Methods: The system integrates a pneumatic-hydraulic actuation unit, multi-camera optical tracking, and a CT-compatible enclosure to replicate and measure intracranial expansion. A phantom head model was fabricated via 3D printing using cranial bones and flexible latex sutures, reproducing neonatal cranial biomechanics. Controlled hydraulic pressure simulates intracranial volume (ICV) growth, while surface and volumetric changes are captured through synchronized imaging. Results: Morphometric parameters - biparietal diameter, occipitofrontal diameter, cranial circumference, and ICV - were measured and compared against published reference data. The system achieved high reproducibility across repeated trials. CT-derived ICV values (R2 = 0.98) closely matched reference trends, with average manufacturing deviations of 0-4 mm between fabricated and reference geometries. Linear morphometric increments confirmed physiologically consistent expansion patterns. Conclusion: The proposed platform provides a quantitatively validated, controllable, and CT-compatible environment for studying neonatal cranial development. It enables biomechanical testing and device evaluation under ethical and repeatable in vitro conditions, with potential future applications in surgical training and pre-operative planning.

papers.title: Biochemical selection on conserved glycans yield a cross-species AAV capsid for efficient panretinal intravitreal delivery
papers.abstract: Inherited retinal diseases are leading candidates for gene therapy, but photoreceptor-directed adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors still require subretinal injection, which treats only part of the retina and carries surgical risk. Intravitreal delivery is simple and panretinal, yet inner-retinal barriers block most capsids, and capsids selected in one species rarely translate. Mapping retinal glycans across seven mammals, we found heparan sulfate (HS) marking the inner limiting membrane and terminal N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) enriched on photoreceptor segments. These invariants defined a two-part design principle, attenuated HS binding with strong terminal GlcNAc engagement, implemented as a sequential in vitro selection, Conserved Receptor-Selection Technology (CReST). Its lead GlcNAc-selected capsid, AAV2.IvtB, increased retinal transgene expression 6.5-fold over AAV2.7m8 in mice and photoreceptor transduction 2.5-fold in pigs, acting through terminal GlcNAc engagement. It partially preserved photoreceptors in rd10 mice and suppressed laser-induced choroidal neovascularization. CReST is a receptor-guided, animal-free route to capsids with a defined, conserved mechanism.

papers.title: ProlateNet: Sampling-rate transfer of convolutional networks with a weights-only certificate for physiological signals
papers.abstract: A central goal of physiological signal analysis is to train a model once and deploy it across recording systems. However, these systems sample EEG and ECG at different rates, and a network trained at one rate loses accuracy at the others. Continuous-kernel networks were built to solve this problem, but published ones still fail at unseen rates, and no existing method can certify a trained model before deployment. In this study, we propose ProlateNet, which builds kernels from prolate spheroidal wave functions to suppress aliasing across sampling rates and certifies a trained model from its weights alone. Across fourteen first-layer designs trained at one rate on three public EEG and ECG datasets, the published continuous-kernel layers FlexConv and sampling-frequency-independent (SFI) convolution show mean worst drops of 0.18 and 0.35 macro-F1 on SEED. ProlateNet is the only design that is stable and accurate on all three datasets with an error bound fixed before training, and its mean worst drop is at most 0.003. Without target-rate recordings, its certificate ranks the continuous-kernel designs on SEED by measured transfer with Spearman {rho} = 0.92, against 0.68 for energy above the training Nyquist frequency. Overall, ProlateNet shows that controlling aliasing enables convolutional networks to transfer across sampling rates and provides principled guidance for building physiological signal models that are trained once and deployed across recording systems.

papers.title: Membrane Biofouling and Plasmid Conformation Shape the Retention of Antibiotic Resistance Gene-Carrying Plasmids during Ultrafiltration
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance poses a growing threat to human and environmental health, and wastewater treatment plants are important pathways for the release of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). Although ultrafiltration (UF) membranes effectively retain antibiotic-resistant bacteria, their capacity to remove extracellular ARGs remains less understood. Extracellular plasmids are concerning because they persist following cell lysis and may contribute to horizontal gene transfer. Unlike intact bacterial cells, these flexible DNA molecules may pass through membrane barriers. Here, we investigated the removal of extracellular plasmids carrying ARGs using a 100 kDa molecular weight cut-off (MWCO) UF membrane, focusing on biofouling, plasmid size, and conformation. Initial filtration experiments achieved removal efficiency (RE) above 99.9% for antibiotic-resistant bacteria and plasmids, and produced a pronounced biofouling layer. For the pre-fouled membrane, mass balances showed increased adsorption and permeation of plasmids, with RE declining from approximately 99% to below 95% over consecutive runs. Microscopy indicated plasmid deposition in biofouled regions. Additionally, plasmid size showed no consistent relationship with RE, while conformation had a pronounced effect, with supercoiled plasmids being retained more efficiently (98.8-99.6%) than their linear counterparts (82.4-92.4%). These findings demonstrate that plasmid retention by UF is influenced by both membrane conditions and DNA conformation, which nominal membrane pore size alone cannot capture. The high RE highlights the potential of UF as a tertiary treatment, while emphasizing the need to account for biofouling and DNA structural diversity when evaluating strategies to reduce extracellular ARG discharge from wastewater treatment plants.

papers.title: Force Volume Atomic Force Microscopy of THP-1 and Primary Mouse Macrophages Reveals that the Mechanical Signature of Macrophage Polarization is Model-Dependent
papers.abstract: Macrophages are immune cells with a rich morphological variety and markedly different biological functions when differentiated into M0 (non-activated) macrophages or polarized into M1 (pro-inflammatory) and M2 (anti-inflammatory) phenotypes. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) studies have recently associated a mechanical dimension with macrophage polarization. Herein, the elastic properties of the three phenotypes are measured and compared by force volume AFM in two less explored models: THP-1-derived macrophages (cell line) and mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs, primary cells). High-indentation measurements (indentation higher than 2 micrometers) with colloidal probes capture the full cell deformation, and a recently derived spherical model with bottom effect correction provides quantitative values of the Youngs modulus (E) that account for substrate effects and cell height with the correct probe geometry. THP-1-derived macrophages show significant mechanical differences, with EM1 higher than EM2 and EM0, whereas BMDMs show no significant differences between phenotypes. Furthermore, BMDM-derived M0 and M2 macrophages show 1.5 to 2 times higher E than the corresponding THP-1 phenotypes. The elasticity of cells with different shapes is also evaluated to account for the heterogeneous macrophage morphology found in all samples. These results indicate that the mechanical signature of macrophage polarization is model-dependent.

papers.title: Dynamic nanocomplexes of antibiotics and biofilm-degrading enzymes overcome biofilm tolerance to treat Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections
papers.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms limit antibiotic penetration and protect embedded bacteria, making established infections difficult to treat. To combat the biofilm, administering tobramycin (Tob) with deoxyribonuclease I (DNase) could pair antimicrobial action with biofilm matrix degradation, but their distinct physicochemical properties hinder co-delivery and transport into the biofilm core. Taking advantage of the acidic biofilm microenvironment, we developed pH-responsive nanocomplexes (NCs) that expand, favoring local retention of the NCs and their cargo. We used stepwise electrostatic precomplexation to co-load Tob and DNase into the NCs, then electrostatically added a PEG-bearing polymer to their surface to improve NC distribution within biofilms, forming PEG-NCs. Across established biofilms of three P. aeruginosa strains, these dynamic NCs overcame biofilm-associated tolerance toward tobramycin and produced the most consistent reductions in bacterial burden and biomass. Formulation-function analyses coupled with biofilm imaging suggested complementary contributions from PEG and active DNase components. In an established murine abscess model, a single intra-abscess PEG-NC injection reduced bacterial burden by approximately 2 log-fold and improved abscess healing, whereas dose-matched Tob and Tob+DNase controls did not significantly improve infection outcomes. Overall, dynamic NCs mediate the co-delivery of biofilm matrix disruptors with antibiotics to improve treatment of established biofilm infections.

papers.title: Short-Duration Fluid Shear Stress Enhances LPS-Driven Macrophage Pro-Inflammatory Response in a Magnitude-Dependent Manner
papers.abstract: Macrophages are mechanosensitive cells that integrate physical and biochemical cues to shape inflammatory responses. Mechanical stimuli such as stretch, strain, and matrix stiffness have been extensively studied; however, the effects of fluid shear stress (FSS) on macrophage function remain relatively poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how mild-magnitude, short-duration FSS applied alone or in combination with Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), affects bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDM) phenotype and function. FSS alone had no effect on naive macrophages, and lower magnitude shear stress did not produce any significant effects under any condition. However, when macrophages were exposed to 0.8 Pa FSS prior to LPS stimulation, tumour necrosis factor (TNF) secretion was significantly increased, and IL-10 production decreased compared with static controls. This magnitude-dependent priming effect was also sequence-specific, as FSS applied after LPS stimulation did not produce any significant changes. These findings demonstrate that mild FSS can mechanically prime macrophages to amplify the inflammatory response but only above a threshold magnitude and when applied before biochemical stimulation. Our results highlight the importance of both shear magnitude and stimulation order in determining macrophage mechanosensitivity, with implications for understanding immune cell behaviour in mechanically dynamic microenvironments and how inflammation can be affected by the mechanical forces in vivo. Keywords: Mechanosensation; fluid shear stress; lipopolysaccharide; inflammation.

papers.title: VINCIT: A virus-incorporated biomaterial niche enables spatially controlled in vivo CAR T cell engineering
papers.abstract: In vivo generation of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells could bypass the complex manufacturing required for conventional cell therapies, but systemic gene delivery remains limited by off target exposure and inefficient access to target immune cells. Here, we develop VINCIT (Virus Incorporated Niche for Cellular ImmunoTherapy), an injectable nanofiber hydrogel composite that establishes a localized immune-engineering niche for CAR T cell generation in vivo. VINCIT spatially retains viral vectors while recruiting endogenous immune cells, enabling local transduction of T cells, after which the engineered T cells enter the circulation. VINCIT spatially confines transgene expression compared with intravenous viral delivery and markedly enhances T cell transduction compared with subcutaneously injected free virus. VINCIT is compatible with both adeno-associated and lentiviral vectors, and CAR T cells generated in vivo exhibit antigen-specific effector responses and mediate CD19+ B cell depletion. In a humanized mouse model of lymphoma, a single VINCIT administration produces sustained tumor control and extends median survival from 32 to 110 days. Mechanistically, efficient CAR T cell generation requires coordinated interactions among multiple immune populations, with neutrophil depletion markedly reducing cellular recruitment and subsequent T cell programming. These findings establish a localized biomaterial niche for spatially controlled in vivo immune cell engineering.

papers.title: ALI MEA60: A porous thin-film microelectrode array for air-liquid interface electrophysiology of 3D excitable tissues
papers.abstract: Objective: Conventional microelectrode arrays (MEAs) are suboptimal for long-term electrophysiology of three-dimensional (3D) excitable tissues, as limited oxygenation, nutrient diffusion, and tissue-electrode coupling compromise recording stability. Air-liquid interface (ALI) culture mitigates these constraints, but existing ALI MEA platforms are limited in channel count, flexibility, and compatibility with commercial multichannel acquisition systems. We developed and comprehensively characterized a next-generation ALI MEA for standardized, long-term recordings across multiple 3D excitable tissue models. Approach: The novel ALI MEA60 is composed of a porous polyimide membrane that integrates an array of 60 thin film microelectrodes (59 recording, one reference) and a basal perfusion chamber with Luer-lock connectors for controlled medium exchange and pharmacological wash-in/wash-out. It is compatible with the MEA2100-Mini data acquisition system (Multi Channel Systems). We characterized electrode impedance and noise across 41 ALI MEA60 devices, assessed 60-day stability with human iPSC-derived neural spheroids (N = 7 MEAs, 121 recordings) using a standardized longitudinal framework and linear mixed-effects models, and evaluated its versatility through pharmacological assays and recordings from human neural spheroids, brain organoids, ex vivo brain slices, and cardiac organoids. Main results: The platform showed reproducible electrical performance (median impedance 56 kOhms; at 1 kHz) and low noise (approx. 5uV Root Mean Square (RMS) in saline, 10-20 uV in medium), resolving spikes and local field potentials simultaneously. Recording remained stable for at least 60 days, with a stable noise floor and ~85% persistence of initial functional channels. Neural spheroids reproduced the standard qualitative signatures to gabazine, 4-aminopyridine (4-AP), and 6-Cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione/D-2-amino-5-phosphonovalerate (CNQX/D-AP5), while cardiac organoids showed the expected beta-adrenergic response to isoproterenol. The ALI MEA60 can similarly record signals from human brain slices and organoids without hardware modification. Significance: The ALI MEA60 combines ALI culture, chronic recording stability, standardized pharmacological testing and cross-tissue compatibility in a single ready-to-use platform. It also establishes a reproducible framework for benchmarking long-term electrophysiological performance, thereby supporting disease modelling, drug discovery, organ-on-chip technologies and future chronic 3D electrophysiology systems. Keywords: microelectrode array (MEA); air-liquid interface (ALI); 3D excitable tissues; neural spheroids; cardiac organoids; chronic electrophysiology.

papers.title: Location of maximum bending stress in tapered hollow plants: A case study on Moso bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis)
papers.abstract: Many slender plants, such as trees and bamboo, have naturally tapered, axially graded forms to withstand wind loads; however, while trees feature solid cross-sections, bamboo culms are hollow. Although tapered hollow stems improve mechanical efficiency, the location at which the maximum bending stress develops remains unclear. As failure in such structures is driven by the bending-induced stress state, identifying this location is essential for understanding their structural capacities. This study aimed to (1) identify the location of the maximum bending stress of a tapered hollow beam made from an axially functionally graded material under various load profiles, (2) verify the consistency between linear and large deflection analyses, (3) investigate the effect of taper ratio on this location, and (4) apply the analysis to Moso bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis) as a case study. Governing nonlinear equations were derived for uniformly distributed load, inverse triangular load, triangular load, and point load; the equations were solved using a large deflection analysis. A linear analysis was also conducted and compared with the nonlinear results. The results showed that the linear analysis is sufficient for predicting the location of the maximum stress under distributed loading; however, under concentrated loading, it is accurate only at low loads. A more tapered geometry shifted the maximum stress toward the tip. In Moso bamboo, the maximum stress is located in the upper region of the culms, providing insights into the natural structural design of tapered hollow plants and a foundation for the design of bio-inspired tapered hollow components.

papers.title: Reprogramming a thiosulfate bacterial two-component system into a perchlorate biosensor
papers.abstract: Engineering bacterial two-component systems (TCSs) to sense new molecules would enable programmable whole-cell biosensors, but retargeting membrane-bound sensor histidine kinases is challenging because ligand recognition and signal transduction are tightly coupled. Here, we reprogram the thiosulfate-responsive TCS from Shewanella halifaxensis (ThsSR) to detect perchlorate, for which no naturally occurring TCS sensor has been reported. Using a dual growth selection, we simultaneously selected for perchlorate-dependent signaling and against native thiosulfate responsiveness. This strategy first converted wild-type ThsS into a perchlorate-responsive generalist and then produced specialized variants with improved sensitivity, greatly reduced thiosulfate response, and discrimination against related oxyanions. We next applied the physicsinformed reinforcement learning design method protCAD to functional intermediates identified by directed evolution. protCAD-selected substitutions further enhanced sensitivity or signaling output in specialized sensors, even in backgrounds that were refractory to additional random mutagenesis and gene shuffling. As a final demonstration, we used the engineered TCS sensor in a whole cell biosensor to detect perchlorate in unsterile environmental samples. Together, these results define a productive division of labor between experiment and computation: directed evolution discovers signaling-competent, specificity-altered sequence space, while computation explores that evolved space more completely to refine performance. This evolution-computational strategy provides a framework for reprogramming TCS biosensors toward non-native analytes.

papers.title: On the formation of lipid nanoparticles and encapsulation of RNA: kinetics, dynamics, and self-assembly regimes
papers.abstract: RNA-containing lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) form through self-assembly triggered by micromixing of an organic lipid solution against an aqueous antisolvent, leading to supersaturation and consequent nanoprecipitation. The kinetics of this process remain poorly understood. Here, we employ millisecond-resolved flowthrough small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) coupled to a multi-inlet vortex mixer (MIVM), confined impinging jets mixer (CIJM) and a T-junction mixer, to experimentally investigate the earliest stages of LNP self-assembly. Ordered LNPs show a characteristic high-q feature indicative of the ionizable lipid-RNA complex; changes in the evolution, shape, and intensity of this peak and the overall particle size in the low-q feature reveal changes in particle assembly and RNA cargo encapsulation. Results captured within milliseconds of mixing show that under turbulent flow (water/ethanol ratio 3:1), LNPs are fully formed by as early as 12 ms, including liquid-crystalline internal organization that indicates RNA encapsulation. Adjusting the water/ethanol ratio to 1:1 results in LNPs with a less ordered nanostructure, in line with reports that downstream processing plays a major role in the final structure of particles formed under these solvent conditions. These findings shed light on the mechanisms by which mixing conditions influence LNP formation. We propose a framework of four distinct self-assembly pathways defined by mixing time (i.e. faster or slower than the O(10ms) self-assembly time) and loading strategy (i.e. RNA introduced during the LNP self-assembly step, or in a second step). This provides a basis for understanding how mixing and loading strategies govern LNP formation and homogeneous RNA encapsulation, particularly for high molecular weight RNA payloads. The results establish process-structure-function relationships that support rational optimization for LNP manufacturing processes.

papers.title: Microscopic Neuromodulation with Locally Enhanced Electric Field
papers.abstract: Implantable neural stimulation devices play an important role in fundamental neuroscience research, clinical applications, and emerging technologies such as neuroprosthetics and brain machine interfaces, with increasing demand for spatially precise neuromodulation at cellular and circuit levels. Microelectrode based electrical stimulation relies on charge injection into neural tissue, where irreversible electrochemical reactions at the electrode electrolyte interface may lead to electrode degradation and tissue damage. Although microscale magnetic stimulation provides an alternative, it typically requires sophisticated microcoil architectures and complex fabrication processes. In this work, we introduce a novel neural stimulation mechanism based on localized electric field enhancement. The proposed device employs an electrically insulated sharp metallic tip to concentrate the electric field and generate localized displacement currents capable of activating nearby neurons. Finite element simulations were performed to investigate the underlying stimulation mechanism and establish design guidelines for device fabrication. MEMS based neural probes were subsequently fabricated and experimentally evaluated through in vivo animal studies, with neuronal activation observed at distances of less than 200 micrometers from the probe tip using two-photon imaging. By avoiding Faradaic charge transfer at the tissue interface while offering high spatial localization, orientation selectivity, and a compact device architecture, the proposed approach provides a promising alternative to existing stimulation technologies for chronic and high-density neural interfaces.

papers.title: What a running template needs: leg damping and a hip torque
papers.abstract: A template, the simplest model that reproduces a behaviour, is a hypothesis about what the body must do. For running, the spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) captures the bounce of the centre of mass but not the force behind it: its ground reaction force (GRF) is symmetric in time and always points along the leg. Its many extensions have never faced a common test. We fitted 34 templates to stance GRF and ranked them by the Bayesian information criterion and cross-validation on six open human datasets (414 runner-speed conditions, 2-5 m/s, treadmill and overground) and on aerial running in two guinea-fowl datasets. Every dataset agreed. A running template needs two elements: leg damping, without which errors stayed above 0.3 body weights (BW), and a force off the leg axis, without which the fore-aft error stayed near that of SLIP. In humans, SLIP with leg damping and a hip torque that decays through stance (TD-SLIP) has both; its two-parameter form was best in the three largest datasets and within 9.3 BIC per condition of the best elsewhere (errors 0.15-0.18 BW). Guinea fowl needed the same two elements in another form, a virtual pivot above the centre of mass, and kept it on slippery ground. Parameters varied between runners far more than their gaits, and overground running softened the leg by 8% without changing the ranking: runners share the template's structure, not its numbers. The GRF fixes the template but not how leg and hip share the work, which joint-level data must decide.

papers.title: Long-term low-intensity vibration attenuates age-associated adipogenic bias and enhances osteogenic potential in mesenchymal stem cells
papers.abstract: Aging impairs mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) function and regenerative potential, contributing to a shift in MSCs differentiation away from osteogenesis and toward adipogenesis. This study investigated the effects of in vivo low-intensity vibration (LIV) on bone characteristics, exercise performance, and the functional, mechanical, and molecular phenotypes of bone marrow-derived MSCs from 24-month-old mice. LIV (90 Hz, 0.7 g) was initiated at 5 months and administered twice daily until 24 months. Outcomes were compared with age-matched, non-vibrated controls. LIV was associated with improved voluntary wheel-running performance, including increased running distance and velocity, alongside a trend towards increased trabecular bone volume fraction and trabecular number. MSCs isolated from LIV-treated mice (+LIV) exhibited reduced senescence marker p16 and increased Ki67 proliferation index. +LIV MSCs had increased osteogenic differentiation and mineralization along with upregulated Runx2 and Col1a1 expression. +LIV MSCs exhibited decreased adipogenic differentiation and lipid accumulation, showing downregulated Fasn and Ap2 expression. +LIV MSCs exhibited increased F-actin fiber number, altered vinculin-associated focal adhesions, and increased apparent whole-cell stiffness. Nuclear characterization revealed increased lamin A/C levels and a shift in the storage-loss crossover frequency from 68 to 94 Hz, indicating that elastic-dominant behavior persisted to a higher frequency. These mechanical changes coincided with increased global H3K4me3 and decreased H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 in +LIV MSCs. Collectively, these findings suggest that in vivo LIV is associated with enhanced osteogenic potential in aged MSCs, accompanied by coordinated changes in cytoskeletal organization, nuclear mechanics, and histone modifications, although causal relationships among these changes remain to be established.

papers.title: When fibers crowd: Mesh burden and myofibroblast phenotypes in women with vaginal mesh exposure
papers.abstract: Polypropylene mesh improves the durability of pelvic organ prolapse (POP) repair but can cause complications, most commonly vaginal mesh exposure. Preclinical animal studies demonstrate that mesh deformation increases local mesh burden and is associated with maladaptive remodeling and macrophage-to-myofibroblast transition (MMT). Whether a similar cellular response occurs in women remains unknown. We examined mesh vagina tissue complexes excised from N=17 women with vaginal mesh exposure following sacrocolpopexy. Specimens were stratified into quartiles of mesh burden and evaluated for macrophage density, fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition (FMT) and MMT associated phenotypes, cellular localization relative to mesh fibers, and collagen content and organization. We also interrogated our previously published proteomic atlas, generated from the same institutional mesh excision biorepository, to compare molecular signatures in vaginal tissue from women with mesh exposure, mesh associated pain, or well integrated mesh and controls without mesh. Macrophage density was greater in the highest mesh burden quartile than in the two lowest quartiles. Across all quartiles, approximately 96 to 99% of myofibroblasts coexpressed macrophage markers, consistent with an MMT associated phenotype, and localized near the mesh tissue interface. MMT associated cell density increased numerically with mesh burden, although differences were not statistically significant. Collagen content relative to mesh area was lower in the higher burden quartiles, whereas collagen as a percentage of tissue area did not differ. Proteomic analysis identified alterations in macrophage associated and matrix-remodeling proteins, with prominent changes in exposure specimens. These findings identify a predominant MMT associated myofibroblast phenotype in women with vaginal mesh exposure and link greater mesh burden to heightened macrophage accumulation and reduced collagen relative to implanted material. MMT associated pathways warrant further investigation as potential therapeutic targets for maladaptive mesh remodeling.

papers.title: A field-potential signature of pre-burst dynamics in human higher-order thalamic neurons
papers.abstract: The aperiodic (1/f) component of the local field potential (LFP), long dismissed as noise, is increasingly being recognized as physiologically meaningful. Its exponent has been proposed to index excitation:inhibition (E:I) balance, with higher exponents (steeper spectra) corresponding to greater inhibition. Yet this hypothesis remains debated and has seldom been tested against single-neuron activity. Here, we used rare concurrent single-neuron and LFP recordings from the human pulvinar during goal-directed behavior and quiet wakefulness. Pulvinar recordings in both states revealed signatures of low-threshold calcium spikes (LTS) bursting. Prior work with intracellular recordings have established that LTS bursts require a sustained, spike-free period of hyperpolarization followed by a triggering depolarization, offering a physiologically-grounded test of the E:I hypothesis. We found that the exponent was higher during pre-burst silence relative to duration-matched silent windows preceding tonic spikes. The exponent also reflected the graded nature of burst-priming hyperpolarization: bursts with more constituent spikes followed longer silences and higher exponent peaks. Whereas these relationships held in both behavioral states, co-bursting across neurons exceeded chance only during goal-directed behavior. Co-bursts occurred on a slow (~100 ms) timescale, consistent with a shared cortical input mechanism, and were preceded by a larger rise in the exponent. Together, by linking a field potential measure to a known cellular mechanism, our findings show that the aperiodic exponent tracks the graded priming of thalamic bursts, providing human single-neuron support for the E:I hypothesis.

papers.title: SEA-Lab: Experiment-grounded recursive self-improvement in an automated laboratory
papers.abstract: AI scientists can generate hypotheses, plans, and protocols. Translating these outputs into reliable experiments requires adapting them to local equipment and resources using feedback from observed outcomes. A key challenge is to retain laboratory execution feedback as reusable knowledge for subsequent planning. We present SEA-Lab (Self-Evolving Autonomous Lab), which combines an environment-grounded Dry-Lab Harness that generates protocols and machine-readable procedures, a wet-lab execution harness that coordinates heterogeneous devices and records execution traces and experimental measurements, and a recursive self-improvement mechanism that uses physical feedback to revise reusable execution policies and experimental strategies. Across three rounds of review on 219 tasks, protocol-review pass rates reached 90.41%. On 66 automation-eligible tasks, mean virtual-validation pass rates increased from 16.7% to 87.7% after two revisions. On two liquid handlers, runtime fell by 45.8% for plate replication, 34.1% for well rearrangement, and up to 68.6% for sample normalization. We demonstrated the system in a phage-display experiment linking four automated experimental steps: molecular cloning, phage titration, sample normalization, and ELISA screening. Of 96 starting samples, 93 yielded a sequence-correct clone, and primary ELISA screening identified ten candidates. These results illustrate how laboratory feedback can guide planning around local resources, refine execution on different laboratory instruments, and inform method revision based on experimental results.

papers.title: CUSTOM-Muscle: Customisable, Shape-Tuneable, Oriented Modular PDMS Scaffolds for Disease-Relevant 3D Skeletal Muscle Engineering
papers.abstract: Modelling skeletal muscle in vitro offers a powerful approach for studying muscle physiology and disease. Despite their potential, current models offer limited scope to combine customisable three-dimensional architecture and mechanical support with complementary functional readouts. Many also lack key features of native muscle, including cellular maturation, neuromuscular organisation and a physiological mechanical environment, limiting their ability to recapitulate muscle structure and function. Here, we establish a three-dimensional (3D) miniaturised, customisable and multifunctional platform for human neuromuscular tissue engineering. We developed an entirely open-source pipeline combining computer-aided design (CAD), stereolithography (SLA) and fused deposition modelling (FDM) to generate culture platforms with tuneable 3D geometries and mechanical properties, supporting short- and long-term culture. Across the configurations tested, all platforms supported skeletal muscle differentiation and functional assessment of twitch and tetanic forces. Integration with motor neuron cultures enabled the generation of neuromuscular constructs suitable for live imaging, metabolic analyses and identification of putative neuromuscular contact sites. Furthermore, the platform recapitulated aberrant nuclear elongation associated with muscle laminopathies, enabling quantitative assessment of disease-associated nuclear morphology. Finally, to address the critical role of mechanical stimulation in muscle physiology, we designed and fabricated an integrated platform for controlled mechanical elongation of 3D skeletal muscle constructs. By combining architectural and mechanical customisation with complementary functional readouts, this framework enables experiments tailored to how tissue organisation, intercellular interactions and external mechanical cues shape muscle function and disease. Its open-source foundation provides a route to wider adoption and adaptation across tissue engineering and the biosciences.

papers.title: SLIM-2PF: a miniature two-photon fiberscope for multi-depth neuroimaging in freely moving mice
papers.abstract: Miniaturized two-photon (2P) fiberscopes enable subcellular-resolution imaging of neural activity in freely moving rodents. However, integrating multi-depth scanning into such probes without compromising their high resolution and minimal mechanical load on the animal remains challenging. Here we report a subcellular-resolution, lightweight, multi-depth-scanning 2P fiberscope (SLIM-2PF). It combines an electrowetting lens with high-numerical-aperture distal optics, achieving lateral and axial resolutions of 0.76-0.81 m and 6.4-6.8 m, respectively, across an 84-m depth range, with a field of view of 168 m in diameter. By controlling the focus off-head through a thin copper-wire bundle, we reduced the probe weight to only 1.6 g while retaining a flexible tether. In freely moving mice expressing GCaMP6m in pyramidal neurons of the somatosensory cortex, we implemented two multi-depth imaging modes on the same probe: dual-plane recording of dendritic and somatic activity at 3 Hz per plane, and cross-sectional imaging of an unwrapped cylindrical surface spanning 60 m in depth within each frame at up to 4 Hz, to our knowledge the first demonstration of this mode in freely moving animals. These results establish the SLIM-2PF as a lightweight platform for probing how neural activity is organized across cortical depth during natural behavior.

papers.title: Circular-Arc Modal Migration for Ultrasound Imaging--Part II: Simulation and Experimental Evaluation in Compact Semicircular and Convex Arrays
papers.abstract: Circular-arc ultrasound imaging requires reconstruction that accounts for curvature and offset transmit sources across a wide field. This study evaluates how Circular-Arc Modal Migration (CAMM) changes point-response width, image-energy distribution, and low-echo target separation relative to delay-and-sum (DAS). CAMM combines angular modal analysis, local spectral remapping, and radial synthesis, with the offset phase evaluated through phase screens or approximated by scalar pullback. Guided by Part I's error analysis and point-target comparisons, paired reconstructions use scalar pullback for compact semicircular cyst simulations and phase screens for acquisition-matched C5-2v simulations, six phantom records, and two carotid views from one participant. Each DAS/CAMM pair uses identical RF. The principal observation is that lower energy fractions outside a fixed neighborhood can coexist with broader tangential responses. In C5-2v point simulations, the full-field fraction is lower at 23 of 24 locations, whereas tangential width is greater at all 24. Semicircular cyst contrast improves in most configurations, with reversed ranking at the smallest target. All eight C5-2v cyst configurations at 10--15-mm radial depth favor CAMM in the three contrast measures; deeper comparisons depend on location and metric. Measured reflectors show the same width--energy-fraction pattern, and the evaluated phantom cyst and carotid lumen regions show improved contrast. At 512 x 513 pixels and 24 transmissions, median host latency is 29.79 ms for DAS and 51.87 ms for CAMM on an RTX 4090. The tested CAMM implementation therefore provides regional gains in low-echo target separation alongside broader tangential responses and higher computational cost.

papers.title: Human embryo-informed niche design enables defined bioprinting of undifferentiated hiPSCs
papers.abstract: Bioprinting undifferentiated human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) enables post-printing expansion and lineage specification within geometrically defined constructs, yet the biological cues required to sustain pluripotent cells in a printable 3D microenvironment remain poorly defined. To establish a biologically grounded design framework, we analyzed single-cell transcriptomes from 106 human embryos to identify niche factors associated with pluripotency maintenance. Integrating ligand-receptor inference, pathway enrichment, and published evidence, we identified collagen IV (COL4A1), laminin (LAMA1), fibronectin (FN1), and pleiotrophin (PTN) as candidate niche factors. A minimal alginate-collagen IV-laminin bioink (ACL) supported colony formation, pluripotency, proliferation, and trilineage potential of bioprinted hiPSCs comparably to the MatrigelTM-containing bioink. Incorporating PTN (ACLP) further improved proliferation and survival under deprivation of pluripotency-promoting factors. This improvement was associated with PTPRZ1-dependent AKT signaling, as PTPRZ1 knockdown reduced p-AKT, pluripotency marker expression, and cell viability. Finally, the defined bioink supported printing of three embryo-inspired geometries: inner cell mass, bilaminar disc, and primitive streak. Collectively, this study establishes a single-cell embryo-informed strategy for rational bioink design and enables Matrigel-free bioprinting of undifferentiated hiPSCs.

papers.title: Magnetic field-based actuator-sensor assembly for dynamic mechanical loading and functional analysis of engineered heart tissues in culture
papers.abstract: Cultured ex vivo and stem cell-derived cardiac tissues have emerged as promising tools for discovering mechanisms of human disease, for pharmacological testing and for elucidating mechanisms of genetic cardiac diseases. The current culture systems for these tissues do not fully recapitulate the mechanobiological environment of cardiac tissue or allow detailed characterization of muscle function in culture, which limits the interpretation of these models. To address this methodological gap, we present an integrated electromagnetic actuator chamber (EMC) that modulates preload and afterload independently in engineered heart tissue (EHT) in culture. Because the load can be adjusted online, the system enables longitudinal monitoring of passive mechanical properties, including viscosity and elasticity. Combining these tissue-specific properties with measurement of muscle displacement by high-sensitivity magnetic field detectors and pre-calibrated electromagnetic force, the system provides simultaneous data on displacement and absolute contractile force. With independent modulation of preload and afterload, it enables switching from auxotonic to isometric contraction and determination of length-dependent activation, and these can be tracked over time during culture. To our knowledge, no earlier system combines independent, freely adjustable control of both preload and afterload with continuous, calibrated functional readout in culture, making it possible to study how mechanical load shapes cardiac tissue function, maturation and disease development.

papers.title: QuickXL: An Open-source Ultraviolet Irradiation Device with Programmable Exposure and Active Cooling for Nucleic Acid Crosslinking
papers.abstract: Accessible and reproducible ultraviolet (UV) exposure is important for many chemical and biochemical applications. We describe an open-source laboratory irradiation device designed for psoralen-mediated RNA photocrosslinking, a valuable tool for nucleic acid structure determination. The device is based on 24 nominally 365-370 nm light-emitting diode modules arranged as two selectable 12-emitter series arrays with separate drivers. A Nano-compatible microcontroller, four pushbuttons and an OLED display provide user-programmable light-on and light-off intervals and an elapsed-time limit. The arrays share a fan-cooled aluminum heatsink and sample chamber, and the device can operate inside a 4 {degrees}C refrigerator to limit sample warming. A 3D-printed enclosure incorporates a sliding cover and interchangeable tube and microplate configurations with an approximately 10 mm emitter-to-sample spacing. The design supports inexpensive, configurable irradiation for nucleic-acid sample preparation, and can be adapted for other light-triggered activation of biological samples.

papers.title: Programmable Imaging of Locus-Specific DNA Repair Dynamics Reveals Chromatin-Controlled Therapy Resistance in Cancer
papers.abstract: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) pose a significant threat to genomic integrity, and their efficient repair is critical for cell survival. However, the spatial and temporal aspects of the repair process at specific genomic loci remain a mystery. To address this gap, we developed a novel live-cell imaging platform called Genomic Locus Imaging and DSB Repair Monitoring by Elastin-like Proteins (GLIDRE). This system leverages a CRISPR-guided elastin-like protein (ELP) droplet approach to specifically label non-repetitive genomic loci and enables real-time analysis of repair-associated dynamics at the same site. Using GLIDRE, we demonstrate that DSB repair-associated dynamics are significantly faster in open chromatin regions compared to compacted regions, irrespective of local transcriptional activity, supporting a model in which chromatin accessibility defines the baseline response whereas transcriptional activity acts in a context-dependent manner. In a model of diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG), the H3.3K27M mutation reshapes chromatin accessibility and repair dynamics in a locus-specific manner. At the tumor suppressor locus CDKN2A, H3.3K27M mutation caused a more repressive chromatin state and delayed repair-associated dynamics, which was associated with resistance to CAR T-cell therapy. Pretreatment with the histone deacetylase inhibitor suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA) restores repair dynamics at CDKN2A and sensitizes H3.3K27M tumor spheroids to CAR T-cell therapy. Together, our findings reveal chromatin accessibility as a key determinant of DSB repair dynamics and support a mechanistic link and actionable connection between chromatin state, DNA repair, and immunotherapy response.

papers.title: Biomolecular design through latent reasoning with RFD4-Proteina
papers.abstract: Biomolecular design requires finding chemically and geometrically compatible arrangements of interacting atoms and molecules. The complexity of problems which can be tackled by deep learning design models is limited by both the molecular landscape they encompass and their ability to explore that landscape effectively. Here we introduce RFD4-Proteina, which addresses these limitations through intrinsic and extrinsic reasoning within a shared chemical and conformational latent space. The latent space encompasses standard and modified amino acids, sugars, DNA, and RNA, with force-field supervision favoring physically plausible atomic reconstructions. Within this space, intrinsic reasoning uses recurrent refinement to adaptively allocate computation, while extrinsic reasoning guides search with arbitrary constraints such as energetic or geometric criteria. Across in silico protein design benchmarks, RFD4-Proteina achieves higher design success rates at greater generation throughput than all previous methods evaluated, with further gains from conformational flexibility, recurrent refinement, and search. The same model performs equivalently to or better than state-of-the-art specialist methods for side-chain packing, sequence design, conformational sampling, and design refinement. We demonstrate the power and versatility of RFD4-Proteina experimentally by designing specific and cross-reactive binders to therapeutically relevant targets, recognizing phosphorylations, controlling glycosylation, and creating enzymes that catalyze both bond-breaking and bond-forming reactions, including a first proof-of-concept demonstration of a de novo designed enzyme for active pharmaceutical ingredient synthesis. By unifying diverse chemistry, conformational flexibility, and scalable reasoning in a single physically grounded latent space, RFD4-Proteina expands the frontier of biomolecular design.

papers.title: Restriction Enzyme activity under Force determined with autonomous DNA Origami Force Clamps via Gel Electrophoresis
papers.abstract: Investigating force-depending behaviour in biological systems is a challenging task, with most techniques requiring complex experimental equipment while also often being limited in scalability. We designed a facile force spectroscopy technique using DNA origami-based force clamps that apply forces up to ~40 pN. We validated the approach by using type II endonucleases that have been previously studied quantitatively by single-molecule measurements. Using ensemble measurements based on ubiquitously used agarose gel electrophoresis, we qualitatively observed force-dependent behaviour for EcoRV and force-independent behaviour for BamHI, replicating previous data for these enzymes. Interestingly, we also observed force-dependent behaviour for EcoRI, whose restriction behaviour has been previously described as force-independent. Our experimental design opens a path to force spectroscopy based on bottom-up techniques and ensemble measurements, allowing to collect statistical data in large quantities with readily available techniques in many wet labs.

papers.title: A Three-Dimensional Bioprinted Skin Melanoma Model for High-Throughput Drug Screening
papers.abstract: Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer, and despite major advances in immunotherapy and targeted therapies, most patients with advanced disease eventually develop treatment resistance. The lack of physiologically relevant, scalable preclinical models that recapitulate the tumor microenvironment (TME) remains a major barrier to identifying more effective therapies. Here, we present a novel high-throughput screening platform based on a bioprinted, full-thickness human melanoma skin model that combines the biological complexity of native skin with the scalability required for drug discovery. The 3D tissue construct comprises a dermal region containing primary human dermal fibroblasts, melanoma tumor-like cell clusters localized at the dermal-epidermal interface, and an overlying differentiated epidermis composed of primary human keratinocytes cultured at the air-liquid interface, thereby recapitulating key structural and cellular features of the melanoma TME. To enable multiplexed, high-content analysis, melanoma cells and fibroblasts were engineered to express red and green fluorescent proteins, respectively, allowing automated confocal imaging to simultaneously quantify tumor growth and stromal viability. This dual-readout strategy provides an intrinsic counterscreen to distinguish melanoma-selective compounds from nonspecific cytotoxic agents. The assay was implemented in a 96-well bioprinted format compatible with high-throughput screening of compound libraries across multiple concentrations. Using this platform, we identified compounds that selectively reduced melanoma cell viability while sparing surrounding stromal cells, demonstrating the value of incorporating the TME into primary drug screens. By integrating bioprinting, human tissue engineering, and automated high-content imaging into a scalable workflow, this platform provides a robust and clinically relevant approach for melanoma therapeutic discovery and has the potential to improve the translation of preclinical findings into effective treatments for advanced melanoma.
